California’s above-normal high-tide window is underway November 22–27, 2026, with another forecast for December 22–26. For people living or working near the shore, those dates bring an increased risk of coastal flooding. The warning follows record water levels in October, when NOAA gauges measured their highest readings ever at four California locations. ## California record water levels: what drives the flood risk

Three influences combined to push water higher. First, a perigean spring tide occurred when the moon was full and closest to Earth. Spring tides can also occur at new moon, when the sun, moon and Earth align. The alignment increases the gravitational pull on the ocean and can produce higher-than-normal tides. Second, El Niño-driven Kelvin waves carry pulses of warm water east across the Pacific toward the Americas. NOAA says these waves can temporarily raise sea levels along the West Coast by 6–12 inches or more over several weeks. They move slowly, so their sea-level effects can persist and coincide with high tides. Third, an ongoing marine heatwave warmed the water. Warmer water expands and takes up more room, a process called thermal expansion.

“Surf continues to build and will peak this afternoon and evening — including during a lower high tide late this evening. Stay well away from the water’s edge as large waves could suddenly form,” the forecasting service said on social media.
